newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: W. Australia miners brace for new royalty on gold.
newsitem.headline: W. Australia miners brace for new royalty on gold.

text.p: Western Australian gold miners are bracing for the possibility that for the first time they will be forced to pay a royalty on gold production.

State premier Richard Court in handing down Western Australia's 1997/98 (July/June) budget on Thursday is expected to introduce the tax, based on an initial 1.25 percent from January 1, 1998, rising to 2.5 percent by July 1999.
But gold miners have vowed to fight the levy, claiming it would do more harm than good.
"On this issue, I don't think it's dead yet," Cliff Harding, managing director of General Resources NL, which mines the Mount Monger gold lode in the state's eastern goldfields.
A spokesman for Court declined to comment on the the state's final position on the royalty, which is seen as a way of compensating for a shortfall in Federal funds next financial year.
Miners have complained that the implications of the royalty on the state's economics has not fully been thought out by the government.
"There may be a case for something, but not the extent they are talking about," Harding said.
"We're not going to take this lying down," another mining company executive said.

An industry forum committee headed by Peter Lalor, managing director of Gwalia Consolidated Ltd, which mines about 500,000 ounces of gold a year, has been meeting in recent weeks with the government in an effort to discourage introduction of the royalty.
Lalor was not available for comment.
Concerns among miners over a royalty were fuelled by remarks earlier this year by state resources minister Colin Barnett that the royalty could run as high as five percent.
Studies commissioned by the mining industry say a royalty would reduce gold production and ultimately cost the state money.
Western Australia produces about 70 percent of Australia's annual gold production of nearly 300 tonnes.
